PHQ9: Little interest or pleasure in doing things
Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much
Feeling tired or having little energy
Feeling bad about yourself, or that you are a failure or have let yourself or your family down
Trouble concentrating on things, such as reading or watching television
Moving or speaking so slowly that other people could have noticed, or the opposite: being so fidgety or restless that you have been moving around a lot more than usual
Thoughts that you would be better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way
GAD2: Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge
Not being able to stop or control worrying
MOM_TIPS: Sleep is treatment. Hand off one night feed (pumped milk or formula is fine) so you get one 4 to 5 hour stretch.
Eat every few hours: keep easy food where you feed the baby, like nuts, cheese, yogurt, fruit and a water bottle.
Get daylight. A 10-minute walk with the stroller counts, and it's on your step plan.
Say yes to help, and be specific: "Can you bring dinner Tuesday?" or "Can you hold her while I shower?"
Lower the bar. A fed baby and a rested mom matter more than a clean house or thank-you notes.
Tell one person the truth about how you feel. Saying it out loud takes away some of its power.
Bring it up at your checkups. Your OB, midwife and your baby's pediatrician all screen new mothers and want to hear it.
Limit the scroll. Other people's highlight reels aren't real life with a newborn.
PARTNER_TIPS: Know her warning signs: crying most days after two weeks, not sleeping when she could, saying she's a bad mother, pulling away from the baby or from you.
Take a night shift. Protecting one long stretch of her sleep is the most useful thing you can do.
Do the work without being asked: dishes, laundry, diapers, bottles, meals.
Be the gatekeeper. Keep visitors short, and send home anyone who stays too long or brings advice instead of help.
Go with her to appointments, and if she's struggling, help her make the call.
Look after yourself too. Fathers get postpartum depression; irritability, anger, working late, drinking more or numbness are signs.
Bond with the baby your way: skin to skin, bath time, walks and the late-night feed.
Talk to another dad, a friend or your pastor. You don't have to be the strong one alone.
SUPPORTER_TIPS: Bring food, not just visits. Set up a meal train with your church, small group or friends.
Offer something specific: "I'll come Thursday 2 to 5 so you can nap" beats "Let me know if you need anything."
Hold the baby so she can shower, sleep or eat, and then leave when you said you would.
Do one chore every time you visit: dishes, a load of laundry, taking out the trash.
Listen more than you advise. "That sounds really hard" helps more than "In my day…"
Ask the dad or partner how he's doing too, and offer him a break.
Keep checking in after the first month, when the meals stop and the visits slow down. Postpartum depression often shows up later.
If you see warning signs, say it gently: "You don't seem like yourself. Can I help you call your doctor?"
HOW_TO_ASK: "How are you really doing, not the baby, you?"
"What's been the hardest part this week?"
"Have you been able to sleep when you get the chance?"
"Have you had any scary or dark thoughts?" Asking doesn't put the idea in someone's head; it lets them answer honestly.
BODY_WARNING_SIGNS: Heavy bleeding that soaks through one or more pads in an hour, clots bigger than an egg, or foul-smelling discharge
A headache that won't go away or gets worse, dizziness or fainting, or vision changes
Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a fast or irregular heartbeat: call 911
Swelling, redness, pain or warmth in one leg or arm
Extreme swelling of your hands or face
Severe belly pain that doesn't go away, or severe nausea and vomiting
Overwhelming tiredness, or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
These can happen up to a year after birth. Get care right away and say "I had a baby in the last year."
WARNING_SIGNS: Sad, empty or crying most days for more than two weeks
Can't sleep even when the baby sleeps, or sleeps all the time
Says she's a bad mother, or that the family would be better off without her
Pulls away from the baby, family or friends
Constant worry, panic, or scary thoughts she can't shake
Talks about hurting herself or the baby: get help now, call 988 or 911

CONDITIONS.title: Baby blues
CONDITIONS.body: Up to 4 in 5 new mothers have tearful, moody, overwhelmed days in the first two weeks. It passes on its own with rest and support. If it lasts longer than two weeks, or gets heavier, it may be postpartum depression.

CONDITIONS.title: Postpartum depression
CONDITIONS.body: About 1 in 7 mothers, any time in the first year. Sadness or emptiness most days, losing interest, feeling like a bad parent, pulling away, trouble bonding, or feeling numb. It's a medical condition, not weakness or a lack of faith, and therapy, support and sometimes medicine treat it well.

CONDITIONS.title: Postpartum anxiety and OCD
CONDITIONS.body: Racing thoughts, constant worry, dread, panic, or unwanted scary thoughts about the baby being hurt, with checking and avoiding. Having these thoughts doesn't mean you want them to happen. It's common and very treatable.

CONDITIONS.title: Depression in fathers and partners
CONDITIONS.body: About 1 in 10 new fathers, often 3 to 6 months after the birth, and more likely when the mother is depressed. It often looks like anger or irritability, working longer, withdrawing, drinking more, or numbness rather than sadness.

CONDITIONS.title: Postpartum psychosis: an emergency
CONDITIONS.body: Rare (1 or 2 in 1,000 births), usually in the first weeks. Confusion, seeing or hearing things that aren't there, paranoid or strange beliefs, not sleeping for days without feeling tired, or very fast mood swings. Call 911 or go to the emergency room. Don't leave her alone with the baby. It's treatable, and recovery is the rule.

MOM: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
PARTNER: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
SUPPORTER: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

PRAYERS.MOM: Lord, I'm tired in ways I didn't know were possible. Hold me the way I hold this baby. When I feel like I'm failing, remind me that you are gentle with those who have their young. Give me rest, give me people who help, and give me the courage to ask for it. Amen.
PRAYERS.PARTNER: Lord, help me carry this season well. Give me patience in the night, eyes to see when my partner is struggling, and the humility to ask for help when I am too. Make our home a place of rest. Amen.
PRAYERS.SUPPORTER: Lord, show me how to love this new family in practical ways. Let me bring help, not advice, and notice what they need before they have to ask. Watch over them in the long nights. Amen.

COMFORT: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
FAITH_NOTE: Struggling after a baby isn't a lack of faith. Prayer and good medical care work together: seeing a doctor or counselor is one way God answers.
EMERGENCY: If you or your baby are in danger, or someone shows signs of postpartum psychosis, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.
SLEEP_NOTE: With a newborn, count trouble sleeping even when the baby is asleep, or feeling drained in a way rest doesn't fix.
